screens.title: SD-Access Overlay: VXLAN and LISP Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by grounding what the SD-Access overlay actually does and why two protocols are required. The overlay sits logically over a working IP underlay. VXLAN is the data plane mechanism that carries Ethernet frames across that underlay by encapsulating them with a VXLAN header, UDP, and an outer IP header. LISP is the control plane that registers endpoints and resolves where those encapsulated packets should be sent. Together they separate identity and location: the endpoint keeps the same IP identity while the fabric tracks where it currently lives. In practice this lets hosts move between fabric edge nodes without changing addresses or the underlay routing. A concrete example is a user laptop that keeps the same IP when moved from one office to another; the new edge node updates the LISP mapping and VXLAN sends the traffic to the new location. A common misconception is that the underlay must be aware of endpoint identities — it does not. The underlay only routes outer IP addresses, the RLOCs. This chapter will show you the encapsulation steps, how VNIs create millions of logical segments, how LISP registers EID-to-RLOC mappings, and practical troubleshooting checks such as looking at MAP entries and verifying VXLAN encapsulation. As you proceed, notice how identity, location, and encapsulation are kept separate, and think about how that separation simplifies mobility and scale.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain VXLAN as the overlay data plane, describe how VNIs create isolated virtual networks, and detail how LISP operates as the control plane. You will learn to distinguish Endpoint Identifiers from Routing Locators and to articulate how their separation enables host mobility. For each objective you will practice by tracing an actual packet flow and examining Map-Server entries where LISP stores EID-to-RLOC mappings. For example, describing VXLAN involves naming the encapsulation sequence and explaining what the outer IP header represents in the underlay. Describing VNIs requires understanding the 24-bit identifier and why VLAN limits are no longer restrictive. Explaining LISP means showing how an Edge Node registers its EIDs with the Fabric Control Plane Node and how map queries resolve RLOCs. Finally, you will tie these pieces together with a mobility scenario where an endpoint moves between edge nodes and the control plane updates mappings without readdressing. These objectives are chosen so you can both reason about the design and verify it in a live fabric.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on the applied skills you will build. You will practice tracing an endpoint-to-endpoint packet through registration, query, encapsulation, transport, and de-encapsulation. Specifically, you'll inspect the Fabric Control Plane Node's mapping database and confirm that registrations exist for active EIDs. You'll use command-level verification such as checking LISP EID tables and confirming VXLAN interface encapsulation state. A practical exercise in the chapter asks you to step through a scenario where Endpoint A with a VNI communicates to Endpoint B in another VNI and the Anycast Gateway is used for inter-VNI routing. This will teach you what protocol is active at each stage: LISP for map resolution, VXLAN for packet transport, and the underlay for routing outer IP headers. You will also practice diagnosing common errors such as wrong VNI assignments or MTU-related fragmentation by checking interface MTU and ensuring underlay supports VXLAN overhead. By practicing these steps you gain confidence not only in identifying faults but also in understanding which plane is the source of the issue.

screens.title: What is VXLAN and why it is the overlay data plane
screens.narratorSegment: VXLAN stands for Virtual Extensible LAN and in SD-Access it serves as the overlay's data-plane tunneling mechanism. At its core VXLAN takes the original Ethernet frame from an endpoint and wraps it with a VXLAN header, a UDP header, and an outer IP header. The outer IP header carries the RLOC addresses of fabric edge nodes. This encapsulation allows Layer 2 segments to be extended across Layer 3 underlays without relying on VLAN limits. A concrete example: when a PC sends a frame to another host in the same virtual network, the fabric edge node encapsulates that frame in VXLAN and sets the VNI so that the receiving edge node can deliver the frame into the correct virtual segment. The VNI is a 24-bit identifier that supports millions of distinct segments, which solves the scaling limitation of 4,094 VLANs. A common misconception is thinking VXLAN alters the endpoint’s IP; it does not. The inner frame, including the original source and destination IPs, remains unchanged. Instead, VXLAN provides a transport tube across the underlay. In practice you must also account for overhead: VXLAN adds bytes to each packet so the underlay MTU must be sized appropriately to avoid fragmentation. Key takeaway: VXLAN provides scalable Layer 2 extension over any Layer 3 network while preserving endpoint identities.

keyIdea.title: VXLAN Definition
keyIdea.text: VXLAN encapsulates Ethernet frames with VNI, UDP, and outer IP headers so virtual networks can span a routed underlay.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is VXLAN?
Encapsulation that carries Ethernet frames across an IP underlay.
sub-template: definition
Definition

VXLAN wraps an original Ethernet frame with a VXLAN header (containing the VNI), then UDP, then an outer IP header using RLOCs. This lets Layer 2 segments move across Layer 3 fabrics.

Analogy
Think of VXLAN as a truck that carries a package across a highway. The package is the Ethernet frame and the truck's license plates are the RLOCs.
Key Takeaway

VXLAN preserves inner frame details while adding a VNI to maintain logical separation.

Encapsulation Steps (visual)
Inner Frame
Original Ethernet frame with endpoint IPs unchanged.
VXLAN + VNI
Adds 24-bit VNI to identify the virtual network.
UDP + Outer IP
Outer headers use the source and destination RLOCs for routing across the underlay.
Common Mistake
Assuming underlay inspects inner EIDs; the underlay only routes outer RLOC addresses.
Pro Tip
Ensure underlay MTU accommodates VXLAN overhead (typically 1550 or larger).

screens.title: VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) and logical segmentation
screens.narratorSegment: The VXLAN Network Identifier, or VNI, is the 24-bit field inside the VXLAN header that labels which virtual network an encapsulated frame belongs to. Because the VNI is 24 bits long, it supports over 16 million unique segments, which is orders of magnitude beyond traditional VLAN limits. Functionally the VNI isolates traffic: two endpoints on the same physical underlay can belong to different VNIs and never see each other’s Ethernet frames even when their VXLAN-encapsulated packets traverse the same underlay links. A concrete example helps: imagine two departments sharing the same campus network but requiring full isolation. Assign department A VNI 1000 and department B VNI 2000. Even if both sets of encapsulated packets are routed through the same underlay routers, the VNI ensures frames are delivered only to edge nodes participating in that VNI. A common misconception is equating VNI with an IP subnet — they are related but not identical. VNI is a segment identifier for overlay forwarding; IP addressing still defines endpoint identities. When troubleshooting mis-segmentation check that the VNI assignments on both source and destination edge nodes match and that any inter-VNI policies (like Anycast Gateway behavior) are intentional. Key takeaway: VNI provides scalable, explicit segmentation so overlays can host many isolated tenant or application networks.

keyIdea.title: VNI Role
keyIdea.text: The 24-bit VNI uniquely identifies a virtual network so many isolated segments can coexist on a shared underlay.

content.html:
Definition
VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI)
A 24-bit overlay tag that creates logical segmentation across the fabric.
sub-template: definition
How VNIs work
  • • VNI is carried in the VXLAN header to tag overlay traffic for a specific virtual network.
  • • It preserves isolation even when multiple VNIs share the same underlay path.
  • • VNIs decouple segmentation from physical VLAN limits, enabling large-scale multi-tenancy.
Key Takeaway

Use VNIs to scale segmentation; verify matching VNI on both edge nodes to avoid cross-segment leaks.

Concrete Example
Department A uses VNI 1000, Department B uses VNI 2000. Even when traversing the same routers, packets remain segregated by VNI.
Misconception: VNI is not an IP subnet; it is an overlay segment label. IP addressing still identifies endpoints inside that segment.

screens.title: LISP: the control plane that maps identity to location
screens.narratorSegment: LISP — the Location/ID Separation Protocol — is the control plane used in the SD-Access fabric to separate who an endpoint is from where it is attached. The identity is the Endpoint Identifier, usually the endpoint's IP (EID). The location is the Routing Locator (RLOC), typically the loopback IP of the Fabric Edge Node where that endpoint is currently connected. When an endpoint comes up, its fabric edge node registers the EID-to-RLOC mapping with the Fabric Control Plane Node, which implements both Map-Server and Map-Resolver functions. The Map-Server stores mappings; the Map-Resolver answers queries from other edge nodes that need to reach an EID. For example, when Host A wants to talk to Host B, the source edge node asks the Map-Resolver for B's RLOC; once it receives that RLOC, it encapsulates the frame with VXLAN addressing the destination RLOC. A common misconception is that LISP itself forwards traffic — it does not. LISP provides discovery and mapping; VXLAN performs the forwarding. In troubleshooting, check that registrations are present on the control plane and that map-resolve replies contain the expected RLOC. Redundancy for the control plane is important: if the Map-Server is unavailable, new registrations and queries will fail. Key takeaway: LISP is the fabric’s directory service that enables VXLAN transports to reach the right edge node without readdressing endpoints.

keyIdea.title: LISP Role
keyIdea.text: LISP maps EIDs (identity) to RLOCs (location), enabling the fabric to locate endpoints while VXLAN transports their frames.

content.html:
Core Concept
LISP: Location/ID Separation Protocol
A control-plane directory that maps endpoint identities to fabric locations.
sub-template: definition
EID vs RLOC
  • • EID: the endpoint's identity, typically its IP address.
  • • RLOC: the loopback IP of the Fabric Edge Node where that EID is attached.
  • • LISP stores these mappings centrally so edge nodes can find each other.
Why it matters

By separating identity and location, the fabric supports mobility and simplified endpoint management.

Map-Server / Map-Resolver
The Control Plane Node stores registrations and responds to queries so edge nodes can obtain RLOCs for target EIDs.
Misconception: LISP does not forward data; it only resolves and registers mappings.

screens.title: How LISP registration and resolution works
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding LISP requires following two linked processes: registration and map resolution. Registration occurs when an endpoint connects. The Fabric Edge Node learns the EID and sends a map-register to the Fabric Control Plane Node acting as Map-Server. The Map-Server stores this EID-to-RLOC mapping in its database. Later, when another endpoint wants to send traffic to that EID, its local edge node performs a map-request to the Map-Resolver function of the control plane. The resolver checks its database and replies with the RLOC of the destination edge node. Once the source edge node has the RLOC it can form the VXLAN encapsulation with the destination RLOC as the outer IP destination. A concrete example: Host A attaches to Edge1, Edge1 registers 192.168.1.10→10.255.255.1. Host B wants to reach 192.168.1.10; EdgeB queries the Map-Resolver, gets 10.255.255.1, and encapsulates the frame to that RLOC. A common mistake is expecting instantaneous propagation without accounting for control-plane replication or caches; mappings may be cached and need refresh. When troubleshooting remember to check both the Map-Server registration table and the map-cache on the querying node. Takeaway: registration creates the directory entry and resolution retrieves it so VXLAN can carry the frame to the correct location.

keyIdea.title: LISP Workflow
keyIdea.text: Registration writes the EID→RLOC mapping; resolution queries that mapping so the source edge can encapsulate toward the destination RLOC.

content.html:
Process Flow
LISP Registration & Resolution
Two linked steps that enable overlay forwarding decisions.
sub-template: process
Registration (step-by-step)
1. Endpoint connects and Edge Node learns the EID.
2. Edge Node sends a map-register to the Fabric Control Plane Node.
3. Control Plane stores EID→RLOC in its database as Map-Server.
Example: 192.168.1.10 registered to 10.255.255.1
Resolution (step-by-step)
1. Source Edge needs destination EID and sends a map-request to Map-Resolver.
2. Map-Resolver replies with the destination RLOC.
3. Source Edge encapsulates the frame in VXLAN using the received RLOC and VNI.
Tip: caches reduce query traffic but require correct invalidation during mobility.
Common Mistake
Assuming resolution equals forwarding. Resolution only supplies the RLOC used by VXLAN for forwarding.
Check
Verify map entries on the control plane and map caches on edge nodes when flows fail.
Takeaway
Registration + Resolution = directory service for overlay forwarding.

screens.title: VXLAN encapsulation sequence and header roles
screens.narratorSegment: A practical grasp of VXLAN means being able to describe each header added to the packet and why it matters. Start with the inner Ethernet frame: it contains the original source and destination MAC and the endpoint IPs if it's an IP payload. The fabric edge node wraps that frame with a VXLAN header that carries the VNI. That is followed by a UDP header because VXLAN uses UDP as its transport. Finally the edge node adds an outer IP header whose source and destination are the source and destination RLOCs — the loopbacks of the fabric edge nodes. The underlay routers examine and route only this outer IP header. A concrete example: Host A sends a frame to Host B; after resolution, the source edge writes source RLOC 10.255.255.1 and destination RLOC 10.255.255.2 in the outer IP header and sets VNI 100. When the packet reaches the destination edge, that node removes the outer IP, UDP, and VXLAN headers and forwards the original frame on the local segment. A common troubleshooting approach is to confirm the outer IP addresses and the VNI match expected values. If the outer IPs ping but inner traffic fails, check the VNI alignment and map entries. Takeaway: know which header each plane cares about — VXLAN and VNI for overlay semantics; outer IP for underlay routing.

keyIdea.title: Encapsulation Anatomy
keyIdea.text: Inner Ethernet frame → VXLAN (with VNI) → UDP → outer IP (RLOCs). Underlay routes only outer IP.

content.html:
Process Flow
VXLAN Encapsulation Sequence
Which header does what, and who routes it.
sub-template: process
Header Stack
Inner Ethernet Frame
Contains original payload and endpoint identities.
VXLAN Header (VNI)
Labels the virtual network for correct delivery at the destination edge.
UDP Header
Transport for VXLAN over IP.
Outer IP Header (RLOCs)
Source and destination RLOCs route across underlay; inner payload is opaque to underlay.
Example
Host A's 192.168.1.10 encapsulated with VNI 100, UDP, and outer IP 10.255.255.1→10.255.255.2 for transport.
Check: If the outer IPs ping but EID-to-EID traffic fails, validate VNI and LISP mappings.

screens.title: EID vs RLOC — identity and location contrasted
screens.narratorSegment: A core architectural distinction in SD-Access is between Endpoint Identifiers and Routing Locators. The EID is the identity of the endpoint — typically the device's IP address — and it remains stable even when the endpoint moves. The RLOC is the physical or topological locator: the loopback IP address of the Fabric Edge Node that currently hosts the endpoint. Separating these concepts is powerful because it avoids readdressing endpoints or stretching Layer 2 domains to preserve IPs. A concrete contrast: when a laptop moves offices, its EID remains the same; only the RLOC mapping changes in the control plane. This means underlay routing tables do not change and the endpoint keeps existing sessions as long as the control plane updates quickly. A common misconception is thinking RLOCs are per-endpoint addresses; they are per-edge node addresses representing location for many EIDs. When troubleshooting mobility, look at the map-server entries to ensure the EID now points to the new RLOC. Takeaway: identity is stable, location changes — LISP maps the change so VXLAN can forward correctly. EID vs RLOC — identity and location contrasted means eid = who the endpoint is; rloc = where the endpoint is currently located. lisp maps one to the other.. In practical terms, why separating who from where enables mobility and simplified routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
EID vs RLOC
Identity versus location in LISP terminology.
sub-template: comparison
Endpoint Identifier (EID)
  • • Usually the endpoint's IP address.
  • • Represents identity and remains stable across moves.
  • • Used as the destination inside the inner frame.
Routing Locator (RLOC)
  • • The loopback IP of the fabric edge node — a location marker.
  • • Changes when the endpoint moves between edge nodes.
  • • Used in the outer IP header for underlay routing.
Example & Misconception
A laptop keeps IP 192.168.1.10 (EID) but moves from Edge1 to Edge2; only the EID→RLOC mapping is updated. Misconception: RLOC is not per-endpoint; it represents the edge node location.

screens.title: End-to-end packet flow: LISP resolution then VXLAN transport
screens.narratorSegment: Let's trace a complete packet flow using the chapter's scenario to cement how LISP and VXLAN interact. Imagine Endpoint A with EID 192.168.1.10 on Edge Node 1 (RLOC 10.255.255.1) sends a packet to Endpoint B 192.168.2.20 on Edge Node 2 (RLOC 10.255.255.2). First, Edge1 will have registered A's mapping with the Control Plane Node (10.255.255.3). When A sends the packet, Edge1 examines the destination EID and, if it does not have a cached RLOC, queries the Map-Resolver at 10.255.255.3. The resolver replies with the RLOC 10.255.255.2. Edge1 then encapsulates the original Ethernet frame in a VXLAN header with the correct VNI, wraps that in UDP, and sets the outer IP header to source 10.255.255.1 and destination 10.255.255.2. This encapsulated packet traverses the underlay using normal IP routing. When Edge2 receives it, it de-encapsulates the packet, looks at the VNI to determine the virtual network, and forwards the original Ethernet frame to Endpoint B. A common misconception is to think the underlay inspects the inner EID — it does not; it only routes the outer RLOC IPs. Takeaway: resolution must occur before encapsulation so VXLAN can carry the payload to the right RLOC.

sub-template: process
Step-by-step Walkthrough

screens.title: Host mobility in the fabric and LISP updates
screens.narratorSegment: Host mobility is a strong reason to use LISP with VXLAN in SD-Access. Mobility means an endpoint retains its IP address (EID) while physically moving to a different access port or edge node. When the host appears on a new edge node, that edge node registers the same EID with the Fabric Control Plane Node. The Control Plane updates the EID-to-RLOC mapping to reflect the new attachment. Subsequent map-requests from other edge nodes will therefore return the new RLOC, and VXLAN encapsulations will be directed to that new edge node. A concrete scenario: a laptop moves from Office A's Edge1 to Office B's Edge2; the control plane changes the mapping from 10.255.255.1 to 10.255.255.2 and traffic follows without changing the laptop's IP. A common pitfall is forgetting to account for map cache staleness — cached mappings on other edge nodes may still point to the old RLOC and cause transient failures until caches refresh. Another consideration is control-plane availability; redundant control plane nodes ensure registrations and queries continue during failures. Takeaway: mobility is achieved by updating the mapping, not by changing the host's address.

screens.title: Troubleshooting overlay vs underlay: common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting SD-Access requires separating which plane is failing. Start with the underlay: verify RLOC reachability by pinging the loopback RLOC addresses. If RLOCs cannot reach each other, fix underlay routing first. If RLOCs ping but endpoint-to-endpoint traffic fails, the issue is likely in the overlay — either a missing LISP mapping or incorrect VXLAN/VNI configuration. A practical workflow: first confirm LISP registrations on the control plane with a map-server query or by checking the EID table; the chapter recommends checking show lisp eid-table as an example verification. Next, verify the source edge has a map-cache entry or can resolve the destination RLOC. Then confirm that encapsulation uses the expected VNI and that both the source and destination edge nodes have matching VNI configuration. Finally, validate MTU settings because VXLAN increases packet size and can cause fragmentation if the underlay MTU is too small. A common misconception is assuming only the underlay matters; in overlay designs you must check both planes systematically. Takeaway: confirm RLOC reachability, then LISP mappings, then VXLAN/VNI and MTU when diagnosing endpoint reachability problems. Troubleshooting overlay vs underlay: common mistakes means check underlay rloc reachability first, then lisp mappings, then vxlan/vni correctness and mtu to isolate the fault.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Activity: Trace an SD-Access overlay packet flow
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to narrate the same scenario used earlier and specify which protocol and headers are active at each step. Start with Endpoint A generating a frame to Endpoint B. The first visible action is at the source edge: it checks whether it has a map-cache entry. If not, it queries the Map-Resolver — here LISP is active and exchanges map-request and map-reply messages. When a reply returns the destination RLOC, the source edge encapsulates the frame using VXLAN, stamping the appropriate VNI in the VXLAN header, adding UDP, and setting outer IP source/destination to the source and destination RLOCs. The underlay then routes this outer IP packet like any IP flow. At the destination edge, VXLAN, UDP, and outer IP headers are stripped and the original Ethernet frame is delivered to the target EID. A concrete step-by-step expected output would name LISP for steps involving registration or lookup, and VXLAN for encapsulation and de-encapsulation steps. A misconception students often have is mixing which headers are visible on the underlay. The underlay sees only the outer IP and does not need to be aware of EIDs or VNIs. Takeaway: practice writing the protocol active and the header changes at each numbered step to build fluency in reasoning about overlay behavior.

screens.title: Design considerations: control plane HA and MTU planning
screens.narratorSegment: Two operational design considerations stand out: making the control plane highly available, and ensuring the underlay MTU accommodates VXLAN overhead. The Fabric Control Plane Node (Map-Server/Map-Resolver) holds EID-to-RLOC mappings and is critical to overlay operation. If that node becomes unavailable, new registrations will fail and map-requests may not be answered, disrupting communication. Therefore, redundancy—multiple control plane nodes—is standard practice so mappings remain available and queries are answered. Second, VXLAN encapsulation adds extra bytes to each packet. If the underlay MTU is set too small, encapsulated packets can be fragmented or dropped, leading to poor performance or failure. The chapter suggests planning for a 1550-byte MTU or larger to accommodate typical VXLAN overhead. A common misconception is assuming VXLAN avoids fragmentation automatically; in reality, the fabric designer must provision MTU headroom. When designing, include monitoring of map replication and underlay MTU consistency across paths. Takeaway: reliable overlays need both resilient control-plane design and careful MTU planning to avoid performance or availability issues. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Quick Concepts
Key Concepts
EID
The endpoint's identity — often the IP address that stays constant during movement.
RLOC

fullNarratorScript:
We begin by grounding what the SD-Access overlay actually does and why two protocols are required. The overlay sits logically over a working IP underlay. VXLAN is the data plane mechanism that carries Ethernet frames across that underlay by encapsulating them with a VXLAN header, UDP, and an outer IP header. LISP is the control plane that registers endpoints and resolves where those encapsulated packets should be sent. Together they separate identity and location: the endpoint keeps the same IP identity while the fabric tracks where it currently lives. In practice this lets hosts move between fabric edge nodes without changing addresses or the underlay routing. A concrete example is a user laptop that keeps the same IP when moved from one office to another; the new edge node updates the LISP mapping and VXLAN sends the traffic to the new location. A common misconception is that the underlay must be aware of endpoint identities — it does not. The underlay only routes outer IP addresses, the RLOCs. This chapter will show you the encapsulation steps, how VNIs create millions of logical segments, how LISP registers EID-to-RLOC mappings, and practical troubleshooting checks such as looking at MAP entries and verifying VXLAN encapsulation. As you proceed, notice how identity, location, and encapsulation are kept separate, and think about how that separation simplifies mobility and scale.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain VXLAN as the overlay data plane, describe how VNIs create isolated virtual networks, and detail how LISP operates as the control plane. You will learn to distinguish Endpoint Identifiers from Routing Locators and to articulate how their separation enables host mobility. For each objective you will practice by tracing an actual packet flow and examining Map-Server entries where LISP stores EID-to-RLOC mappings. For example, describing VXLAN involves naming the encapsulation sequence and explaining what the outer IP header represents in the underlay. Describing VNIs requires understanding the 24-bit identifier and why VLAN limits are no longer restrictive. Explaining LISP means showing how an Edge Node registers its EIDs with the Fabric Control Plane Node and how map queries resolve RLOCs. Finally, you will tie these pieces together with a mobility scenario where an endpoint moves between edge nodes and the control plane updates mappings without readdressing. These objectives are chosen so you can both reason about the design and verify it in a live fabric.

This second objectives slide focuses on the applied skills you will build. You will practice tracing an endpoint-to-endpoint packet through registration, query, encapsulation, transport, and de-encapsulation. Specifically, you'll inspect the Fabric Control Plane Node's mapping database and confirm that registrations exist for active EIDs. You'll use command-level verification such as checking LISP EID tables and confirming VXLAN interface encapsulation state. A practical exercise in the chapter asks you to step through a scenario where Endpoint A with a VNI communicates to Endpoint B in another VNI and the Anycast Gateway is used for inter-VNI routing. This will teach you what protocol is active at each stage: LISP for map resolution, VXLAN for packet transport, and the underlay for routing outer IP headers. You will also practice diagnosing common errors such as wrong VNI assignments or MTU-related fragmentation by checking interface MTU and ensuring underlay supports VXLAN overhead. By practicing these steps you gain confidence not only in identifying faults but also in understanding which plane is the source of the issue.

VXLAN stands for Virtual Extensible LAN and in SD-Access it serves as the overlay's data-plane tunneling mechanism. At its core VXLAN takes the original Ethernet frame from an endpoint and wraps it with a VXLAN header, a UDP header, and an outer IP header. The outer IP header carries the RLOC addresses of fabric edge nodes. This encapsulation allows Layer 2 segments to be extended across Layer 3 underlays without relying on VLAN limits. A concrete example: when a PC sends a frame to another host in the same virtual network, the fabric edge node encapsulates that frame in VXLAN and sets the VNI so that the receiving edge node can deliver the frame into the correct virtual segment. The VNI is a 24-bit identifier that supports millions of distinct segments, which solves the scaling limitation of 4,094 VLANs. A common misconception is thinking VXLAN alters the endpoint’s IP; it does not. The inner frame, including the original source and destination IPs, remains unchanged. Instead, VXLAN provides a transport tube across the underlay. In practice you must also account for overhead: VXLAN adds bytes to each packet so the underlay MTU must be sized appropriately to avoid fragmentation. Key takeaway: VXLAN provides scalable Layer 2 extension over any Layer 3 network while preserving endpoint identities.

The VXLAN Network Identifier, or VNI, is the 24-bit field inside the VXLAN header that labels which virtual network an encapsulated frame belongs to. Because the VNI is 24 bits long, it supports over 16 million unique segments, which is orders of magnitude beyond traditional VLAN limits. Functionally the VNI isolates traffic: two endpoints on the same physical underlay can belong to different VNIs and never see each other’s Ethernet frames even when their VXLAN-encapsulated packets traverse the same underlay links. A concrete example helps: imagine two departments sharing the same campus network but requiring full isolation. Assign department A VNI 1000 and department B VNI 2000. Even if both sets of encapsulated packets are routed through the same underlay routers, the VNI ensures frames are delivered only to edge nodes participating in that VNI. A common misconception is equating VNI with an IP subnet — they are related but not identical. VNI is a segment identifier for overlay forwarding; IP addressing still defines endpoint identities. When troubleshooting mis-segmentation check that the VNI assignments on both source and destination edge nodes match and that any inter-VNI policies (like Anycast Gateway behavior) are intentional. Key takeaway: VNI provides scalable, explicit segmentation so overlays can host many isolated tenant or application networks.

LISP — the Location/ID Separation Protocol — is the control plane used in the SD-Access fabric to separate who an endpoint is from where it is attached. The identity is the Endpoint Identifier, usually the endpoint's IP (EID). The location is the Routing Locator (RLOC), typically the loopback IP of the Fabric Edge Node where that endpoint is currently connected. When an endpoint comes up, its fabric edge node registers the EID-to-RLOC mapping with the Fabric Control Plane Node, which implements both Map-Server and Map-Resolver functions. The Map-Server stores mappings; the Map-Resolver answers queries from other edge nodes that need to reach an EID. For example, when Host A wants to talk to Host B, the source edge node asks the Map-Resolver for B's RLOC; once it receives that RLOC, it encapsulates the frame with VXLAN addressing the destination RLOC. A common misconception is that LISP itself forwards traffic — it does not. LISP provides discovery and mapping; VXLAN performs the forwarding. In troubleshooting, check that registrations are present on the control plane and that map-resolve replies contain the expected RLOC. Redundancy for the control plane is important: if the Map-Server is unavailable, new registrations and queries will fail. Key takeaway: LISP is the fabric’s directory service that enables VXLAN transports to reach the right edge node without readdressing endpoints.

Understanding LISP requires following two linked processes: registration and map resolution. Registration occurs when an endpoint connects. The Fabric Edge Node learns the EID and sends a map-register to the Fabric Control Plane Node acting as Map-Server. The Map-Server stores this EID-to-RLOC mapping in its database. Later, when another endpoint wants to send traffic to that EID, its local edge node performs a map-request to the Map-Resolver function of the control plane. The resolver checks its database and replies with the RLOC of the destination edge node. Once the source edge node has the RLOC it can form the VXLAN encapsulation with the destination RLOC as the outer IP destination. A concrete example: Host A attaches to Edge1, Edge1 registers 192.168.1.10→10.255.255.1. Host B wants to reach 192.168.1.10; EdgeB queries the Map-Resolver, gets 10.255.255.1, and encapsulates the frame to that RLOC. A common mistake is expecting instantaneous propagation without accounting for control-plane replication or caches; mappings may be cached and need refresh. When troubleshooting remember to check both the Map-Server registration table and the map-cache on the querying node. Takeaway: registration creates the directory entry and resolution retrieves it so VXLAN can carry the frame to the correct location.

A practical grasp of VXLAN means being able to describe each header added to the packet and why it matters. Start with the inner Ethernet frame: it contains the original source and destination MAC and the endpoint IPs if it's an IP payload. The fabric edge node wraps that frame with a VXLAN header that carries the VNI. That is followed by a UDP header because VXLAN uses UDP as its transport. Finally the edge node adds an outer IP header whose source and destination are the source and destination RLOCs — the loopbacks of the fabric edge nodes. The underlay routers examine and route only this outer IP header. A concrete example: Host A sends a frame to Host B; after resolution, the source edge writes source RLOC 10.255.255.1 and destination RLOC 10.255.255.2 in the outer IP header and sets VNI 100. When the packet reaches the destination edge, that node removes the outer IP, UDP, and VXLAN headers and forwards the original frame on the local segment. A common troubleshooting approach is to confirm the outer IP addresses and the VNI match expected values. If the outer IPs ping but inner traffic fails, check the VNI alignment and map entries. Takeaway: know which header each plane cares about — VXLAN and VNI for overlay semantics; outer IP for underlay routing.

A core architectural distinction in SD-Access is between Endpoint Identifiers and Routing Locators. The EID is the identity of the endpoint — typically the device's IP address — and it remains stable even when the endpoint moves. The RLOC is the physical or topological locator: the loopback IP address of the Fabric Edge Node that currently hosts the endpoint. Separating these concepts is powerful because it avoids readdressing endpoints or stretching Layer 2 domains to preserve IPs. A concrete contrast: when a laptop moves offices, its EID remains the same; only the RLOC mapping changes in the control plane. This means underlay routing tables do not change and the endpoint keeps existing sessions as long as the control plane updates quickly. A common misconception is thinking RLOCs are per-endpoint addresses; they are per-edge node addresses representing location for many EIDs. When troubleshooting mobility, look at the map-server entries to ensure the EID now points to the new RLOC. Takeaway: identity is stable, location changes — LISP maps the change so VXLAN can forward correctly. EID vs RLOC — identity and location contrasted means eid = who the endpoint is; rloc = where the endpoint is currently located. lisp maps one to the other.. Let's trace a complete packet flow using the chapter's scenario to cement how LISP and VXLAN interact. Imagine Endpoint A with EID 192.168.1.10 on Edge Node 1 (RLOC 10.255.255.1) sends a packet to Endpoint B 192.168.2.20 on Edge Node 2 (RLOC 10.255.255.2). First, Edge1 will have registered A's mapping with the Control Plane Node (10.255.255.3). When A sends the packet, Edge1 examines the destination EID and, if it does not have a cached RLOC, queries the Map-Resolver at 10.255.255.3. The resolver replies with the RLOC 10.255.255.2. Edge1 then encapsulates the original Ethernet frame in a VXLAN header with the correct VNI, wraps that in UDP, and sets the outer IP header to source 10.255.255.1 and destination 10.255.255.2. This encapsulated packet traverses the underlay using normal IP routing. When Edge2 receives it, it de-encapsulates the packet, looks at the VNI to determine the virtual network, and forwards the original Ethernet frame to Endpoint B. A common misconception is to think the underlay inspects the inner EID — it does not; it only routes the outer RLOC IPs. Takeaway: resolution must occur before encapsulation so VXLAN can carry the payload to the right RLOC.

Host mobility is a strong reason to use LISP with VXLAN in SD-Access. Mobility means an endpoint retains its IP address (EID) while physically moving to a different access port or edge node. When the host appears on a new edge node, that edge node registers the same EID with the Fabric Control Plane Node. The Control Plane updates the EID-to-RLOC mapping to reflect the new attachment. Subsequent map-requests from other edge nodes will therefore return the new RLOC, and VXLAN encapsulations will be directed to that new edge node. A concrete scenario: a laptop moves from Office A's Edge1 to Office B's Edge2; the control plane changes the mapping from 10.255.255.1 to 10.255.255.2 and traffic follows without changing the laptop's IP. A common pitfall is forgetting to account for map cache staleness — cached mappings on other edge nodes may still point to the old RLOC and cause transient failures until caches refresh. Another consideration is control-plane availability; redundant control plane nodes ensure registrations and queries continue during failures. Takeaway: mobility is achieved by updating the mapping, not by changing the host's address.

Troubleshooting SD-Access requires separating which plane is failing. Start with the underlay: verify RLOC reachability by pinging the loopback RLOC addresses. If RLOCs cannot reach each other, fix underlay routing first. If RLOCs ping but endpoint-to-endpoint traffic fails, the issue is likely in the overlay — either a missing LISP mapping or incorrect VXLAN/VNI configuration. A practical workflow: first confirm LISP registrations on the control plane with a map-server query or by checking the EID table; the chapter recommends checking show lisp eid-table as an example verification. Next, verify the source edge has a map-cache entry or can resolve the destination RLOC. Then confirm that encapsulation uses the expected VNI and that both the source and destination edge nodes have matching VNI configuration. Finally, validate MTU settings because VXLAN increases packet size and can cause fragmentation if the underlay MTU is too small. A common misconception is assuming only the underlay matters; in overlay designs you must check both planes systematically. Takeaway: confirm RLOC reachability, then LISP mappings, then VXLAN/VNI and MTU when diagnosing endpoint reachability problems. This activity asks you to narrate the same scenario used earlier and specify which protocol and headers are active at each step. Start with Endpoint A generating a frame to Endpoint B. The first visible action is at the source edge: it checks whether it has a map-cache entry. If not, it queries the Map-Resolver — here LISP is active and exchanges map-request and map-reply messages. When a reply returns the destination RLOC, the source edge encapsulates the frame using VXLAN, stamping the appropriate VNI in the VXLAN header, adding UDP, and setting outer IP source/destination to the source and destination RLOCs. The underlay then routes this outer IP packet like any IP flow. At the destination edge, VXLAN, UDP, and outer IP headers are stripped and the original Ethernet frame is delivered to the target EID. A concrete step-by-step expected output would name LISP for steps involving registration or lookup, and VXLAN for encapsulation and de-encapsulation steps. A misconception students often have is mixing which headers are visible on the underlay. The underlay sees only the outer IP and does not need to be aware of EIDs or VNIs. Takeaway: practice writing the protocol active and the header changes at each numbered step to build fluency in reasoning about overlay behavior.

Two operational design considerations stand out: making the control plane highly available, and ensuring the underlay MTU accommodates VXLAN overhead. The Fabric Control Plane Node (Map-Server/Map-Resolver) holds EID-to-RLOC mappings and is critical to overlay operation. If that node becomes unavailable, new registrations will fail and map-requests may not be answered, disrupting communication. Therefore, redundancy—multiple control plane nodes—is standard practice so mappings remain available and queries are answered. Second, VXLAN encapsulation adds extra bytes to each packet. If the underlay MTU is set too small, encapsulated packets can be fragmented or dropped, leading to poor performance or failure. The chapter suggests planning for a 1550-byte MTU or larger to accommodate typical VXLAN overhead. A common misconception is assuming VXLAN avoids fragmentation automatically; in reality, the fabric designer must provision MTU headroom. When designing, include monitoring of map replication and underlay MTU consistency across paths. Takeaway: reliable overlays need both resilient control-plane design and careful MTU planning to avoid performance or availability issues. These are the concise statements you should be able to recall and explain. VXLAN is the data-plane encapsulation protocol that tunnels Ethernet frames across an IP underlay using a VXLAN header, UDP, and outer IP headers. The VNI is the 24-bit identifier inside VXLAN that isolates virtual networks so thousands or millions of segments can coexist. LISP is the control plane that separates endpoint identity from location: the endpoint's IP is the EID and the edge node's loopback is the RLOC. The Map-Server stores registrations and the Map-Resolver answers queries so sources learn destination RLOCs before encapsulating packets. Host mobility is achieved when a host keeps its EID while the control plane updates its RLOC entry. For troubleshooting, always confirm RLOC reachability first, then LISP mappings, then VXLAN configuration and MTU. These short definitions are meant to be anchors you can apply quickly when verifying overlay behavior in a live fabric.

Here are three more compact concept reminders you will use frequently. EID is the endpoint identity — typically the device IP — and remains stable across moves. RLOC is the routing locator — the edge node loopback — used in outer IP headers for underlay routing. Host mobility is realized when the control plane updates the mapping from EID to a new RLOC, allowing the endpoint to keep its address while the fabric routes to the new location. Keep these short phrases ready: EID equals who, RLOC equals where, and map updates enable mobility. When you encounter connectivity issues, mentally run this checklist: can you reach RLOCs; are EIDs registered correctly; do VNIs match on both edges; is the underlay MTU sufficient? These short rules help you quickly separate control-plane problems from data-plane or underlay problems.
